Maintaining the funds rate at 2.25–2.50% and signaling “patience” is consistent with the Fed’s rule-like behavior (Taylor-rule descriptions and Rudebusch models) and with inflation-forecast targeting frameworks emphasized by Svensson (1997a) and Svensson and Woodford (1999). With market-based inflation compensation low and expectations little changed, the hybrid Phillips curve (Galí and Gertler, 1999) and wage rigidity from nominal contracts (Taylor-style contracts; Christiano and Eichenbaum, 1992b) imply that tight labor markets need not translate into immediate inflation, supporting a pause. The explicit commitment to a symmetric 2% objective reinforces credibility and mitigates inflation bias (Barro-Gordon; Walsh; Goodfriend), while slower household spending and business investment, alongside possible financial accelerator effects, argue against further near-term tightening. Overall, the tone is modestly dovish but still confident in sustained expansion and anchored inflation.
